entries.title: France's Macron says 'illegitimate' protests will be banned in coming days
entries.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to ban unauthorized protests after France was rocked by violence and looting. As anger over public services and the cost of living grows, authorities are bracing for more protests.
entries.content:
France

French President Macron bans 'illegitimate' protests in coming days

October 22, 2026

French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to ban unauthorized protests after France was rocked by violence and looting. As anger over public services and the cost of living grows, authorities are bracing for more protests.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that demonstrations organized by groups without legitimate authority would be banned in the coming days.

Over the past weekend, protests over the education system and the cost of living escalated into violence and looting, which the government blamed on ultra-left groups.

"Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic," Macron said after a special security meeting at the Elysee Palace with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers.

"The general recommendation is not to hold demonstrations in the coming days," he explained. "We want calm to return."

Macron said the ban on protests aimed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.

"Where trade unions submit requests to hold demonstrations, prefects will examine them in accordance with the law, but alternative routes will be proposed," he added.

Fresh demonstration in Paris

In the wake of the past weekend’s violence, several cities had already implemented curfews for certain parts of town. Protests planned Thursday in Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble were banned from going ahead. 

Authorities say a massive security operation was planned for the coming weekend to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s violence. 

Student and university groups as well as unions have said they would continue to mobilize and hold protests. On Thursday, thousands gathered in Paris when a local court was said to have overturned the day's demonstration ban.

France's main student union, UNEF, has called for rallies on Saturday, while the Yellow Vest movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook the country in 2018 and 2019, has filed plans for a march through central Paris.

What are the protests about?

The protests started in September at a school near Paris over lack of funding for the education system.

The demonstrations then spread to other Paris suburbs and eventually to other French cities. They have since widened to also address the soaring cost of living and deteriorating public services.

On October 17, the protests escalated into the worst urban unrest in years when masked rioters clashed with police, looted shops and set cars and buildings on fire.

Two people have been arrested over an arson attack on the 19th-century Limoges city hall, French media reported.

Across France, there were around 2,700 arrests last weekend and hundreds of protesters, police and firefighters were injured. 

French Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said courts jailed 217 people in fast-track trials linked to rioting over the weekend, adding "this figure is continuing to rise a lot."

Macron on Thursday said talks between authorities, student groups, unions, and employers would take place on Monday. He stressed that dialogue over protesters' legitimate demands should continue.

The unrest comes just months before next year's presidential election, in which voters will choose Macron's successor.

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Are the French police the most violent in the EU?
entries.summary: As protests continue in France, the French police are under scrutiny after new allegations of police brutality. The force has a bigger arsenal than most in Europe.
entries.content:
France

Are the French police the most violent in the EU?

October 22, 2026

As protests continue in France, the French police are under scrutiny after new allegations of police brutality. The force has a bigger arsenal than most in Europe.

Videos of alleged police violence are going viral on French social media as a wave of protests grips France. One video shows the police beating a man to the floor then dragging him away unconscious. Another shows an officer grabbing a young man from behind, seemingly unprovoked, and dragging him by the neck. Another shows a young woman being hauled off with a twisted arm, screaming in pain. These videos could not be independently verified. 

The French police have drawn renewed criticism from rights groups, not only because of their methods but also because of their use of stun grenades and rubber bullets. France has one of the most heavily armed police forces in Europe. During the student protests of the past weeks, several teenagers sustained life-changing injuries as a result: One had a hand blown off, one was blinded in one eye, another had his jaw broken. 

France's protests grow

More than half a million people took to the streets in France on Saturday, most of whom protested peacefully, criticizing public sector cuts, the cost-of-living crisis and supporting students' demands for better conditions in classrooms. 

Rioters took advantage, burning buildings, looting stores and lobbing projectiles at the police, creating a difficult situation for the officers and other emergency services.

The protests over the weekend followed a series of protests by high-school students, who barricaded school buildings to denounce a shortage of teachers and demand repairs to crumbling infrastructure. 

More protests will be happening this weekend, with the French government saying it will even deploy military forces.

Weapons made for war?

The French police have a bigger arsenal than most European countries. For instance, officers use the so-called LBD-40, a type of gun used to fire rubber bullets.

Many countries, like the UK and Germany, mostly do not allow the use of rubber bullets in protests. In some European countries, like Spain, they are sometimes used but cause fewer injuries than in France.

"It is not a French specificity. But there are guidelines. There must be a certain distance," Anastassia Tsoukala, an associate professor of criminology at the University of Paris-Sud, told DW. "Even if you try to respect the guidelines, people may move and then all of a sudden they may lose one eye. So it's extremely dangerous."

Police in France routinely use tear gas, as do police in many other countries in Europe. In warfare, its use is actually forbidden under agreements like the Chemical Weapons Convention.

What makes the French police stand out from other forces is its use of stun grenades. 

"These grenades contain a high level of explosive substances. So from this point of view, France is unique," said Tsoukala.

Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez insists that weapons used by the police are "non-lethal." However, some of the equipment used by the force is classified by France's own internal security code as "war material."

French police: the 'most brutal' in the EU?

The police's use of these weapons has received renewed criticism after it resulted in injuries during the protests. The teenager who lost use of an eye is suspected of being hit at close range with a rubber bullet from an LBD-40.

"When we look at crowd control, it is clear that if we measure police brutality by the number of deaths amongst demonstrators or members of the crowd, and if we also measure it by the number of cases of maiming, the French police are the most brutal in the whole of the European Union," says Roche.

He points to the political context to understand the French police's equipment and how it is used today.

"The political authorities are free to decide on the police's equipment," the police expert says. "When LBDs were introduced into the [French] police force, they were intended for units like anti-organized crime units. This is the same weapon that is today used for crowd control. It gives an idea of how the way in which politicians in France think we can or should deal with political protest has evolved."

Confrontation vs. de-escalation

Another difference between the French police and forces elsewhere is the methods. German police, for example, are supposed to try to avoid escalation. 

Roche compares how protestors were moved in Lützerath, Germany, in 2023 to the more aggressive methods in Sainte-Soline, France, in 2023. Both places saw environmental protests.

"In Lützerath, dogs were used, there were some injuries but far fewer seriously injured people on both sides. In Sainte-Soline, the military police was sent in and used LBDs and grenades intensively. There were serious injuries amongst both police officers and demonstrators. Two protestors were left in a coma."

When can police officers use force?

According to international standards set by the United Nations, use of force by officers of the law "should be exceptional," in the case of "prevention of crime" or "lawful arrest." Any use of force should follow a principle of "proportionality," which means no more than necessary to achieve its objective. 

French Interior Minister Nunez has insisted in radio interviews that officers have largely respected this principle, which is also enshrined in French law, during the current protests.

However, rights group Amnesty International describes the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and calls upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations." 

The French branch of the League of Human Rights condemns the "violent repression" of the high school protest movement.

DW contacted two police unions and the French Interior Ministry for comment, but none responded before time of publication.

"It was very complicated to contain all the different groups," Interior Minister Nunez said in Marseille on Tuesday. "The police did a great job and there were a great number of crimes that were prevented thanks to their commitment."

Experts are critical of the police's actions.

"Public order is subordinated to human life and safety," Tsoukala said. "As a jurist I should say that this is a non-negotiable value."

Less oversight than in the UK and Denmark

The French police have no independent watchdog, only an internal division called the IGPN (General Inspectorate of the National Police) that can investigate when problems occur. The IGPN says it has opened at least 40 cases since the beginning of the latest protests.

Countries like the UK and Denmark investigate incidents differently, with independent watchdogs. However, Tsoukala criticizes leniency and a lack of transparency across Europe when incidents with the police occur.

"They are acquitted or they receive extremely light penalties," she said. "And I'm afraid this is the standard method to deal with police brutality cases across Europe."

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: Is Iran ready for another major US attack after midterm elections?
entries.summary: Iranian officials say the goal is to keep the regime in power and threaten enough regional costs to make a prolonged campaign unattractive. US media reports indicate that Trump is considering strikes after the midterms.
entries.content:
Asia

Is Iran ready for another major US attack after midterm elections?

October 22, 2026

Iranian officials say the goal is to keep the regime in power and threaten enough regional costs to make a prolonged campaign unattractive. US media reports indicate that Trump is considering strikes after the midterms.

Officials in Tehran are preparing for renewed strikes 

following media reports that the United States and Israel have been examining new options for escalating their war against Iran.

The US midterm elections on November 3 and Israel's October 27 election have injected a political factor into how both countries are approaching the conflict, which they launched in late February.

Polls show that high energy prices brought on by the Iran war are hurting Donald Trump's Republican Party. On October 8, the president posted on social media that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterms, citing "productive discussions" with Tehran. The United States last launched strikes on Iran in early September. 

After the elections are over, however, Trump may feel less politically constrained.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has campaigned on a platform of regime change in Iran.

Report: Plans in place for 'short' US-Israeli operation

Citing senior US officials the New York Times reported on Wednesday that the United States and Israel have "developed specific plans" for a "short but intensive operation" in Iran that would include targets such as nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure, and the country's arsenal of missiles and drones.

One official told the newspaper that the goal would be to force Iran into making "diplomatic concessions" by further weakening its economy, as negotiations to end the conflict have gone nowhere. The United States has also maintained a blockade of Iranian oil exports in the Strait of Hormuz that has sapped Tehran's oil revenues.

Other outlets have reported similar plans in recent weeks. In early October, Axios reported that the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command "to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran."

There are currently two US aircraft carrier strike groups in the Arabian Sea, with a third expected to arrive by late November.

On October 15, Trump told the right-wing broadcaster Newsmax that he was considering a strike on Pickaxe Mountain, near the Natanz nuclear complex, where US officials say Iran may have moved sensitive nuclear-related material underground.

A day later, CNN reported that Trump is considering using a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb on Iranian targets. As the MOAB creates a humungous blast wave above ground, its effectiveness in targeting underground facilities such as Pickaxe would be limited.

Has Iran learned from earlier attacks?

Iranian officials say they are prepared for another attack, with a broad response that would include strikes on US bases and energy facilities in the Gulf.

Ali Asghar Shafieian, a media adviser to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, told DW that, although the United States retains a significant technological and military advantage, Tehran's strategy is based on preserving the regime's hold on the country rather than matching US strength.

"The United States has the upper hand in military power and technology, but Iran's strength is in how it deals with a crisis," Shafieian said.

Shafieian pointed to the rapid replacement of senior officials killed in previous attacks as an example of how Tehran has tried to make its political structure more resilient. Iran has also been rebuilding missile and drone capabilities that were hit during the massive wave of strikes during the first weeks of the war.

Citing Iranian officials, the Reuters news agency reported this week that Iran is "preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," adding that Tehran was prolonging negotiations to try to weaken Trump ahead of the midterms.

Iran has told regional governments that US military bases and critical infrastructure could become targets if neighboring countries assist another US or Israeli operation.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that participation or cooperation by regional states would result in a "decisive and proportionate response."

"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," Araghchi posted on X Wednesday. "But, if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."

How Iran prepares for new strikes?

Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based political analyst, told DW that Iran's preparations extend beyond missiles and drones to prioritizing internal security.

That includes confronting armed opposition groups, preparing for possible protests and developing plans to prevent external military pressure from combining with domestic unrest.

Another conflict, he said, could bring renewed internet restrictions and a stronger mobilization of government supporters in public spaces.

"In the government's asymmetric-war strategy, the ultimate objective is to convince the United States that regime change through military action is impossible," Ghahremanpour said.

Ghahremanpour added that some factions within Iran have supported returning to a negotiated agreement. But he believes that Washington's demands are now considered so extensive that even Iranian officials who favor compromise struggle to build domestic support for them.

"For now, we are facing a deadlock," Ghahremanpour said. "Iranian officials do not appear optimistic about reaching an agreement."

Talks continue to snag on Iran's nuclear program, which US officials say must top the agenda. 

Iran's latest proposal to the United States, sent through Qatari mediators, included an offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under Iranian control, in exchange for the US's lifting its maritime blockade, releasing frozen assets and ending military actions.

Citing data from the ship tracker Kpler, the Wall Street Journal reported this week that oil flows through Hormuz are approaching prewar levels as the US military escorts tankers and shipping companies are more willing to take risks for a bigger payoff. This raises questions about whether Iran's leverage over oil flows might be weakening.

Fear of war inside Iran

An escalation in the confrontation would come at a moment of severe economic pressure and growing political polarization for Iranians. 

A doctor in Tehran told DW that she fears what would happen should fighting resumed. Speaking with the media in Iran remains very dangerous, and she spoke under condition of anonymity.

"The economic situation has become extremely bad," she said. "Even if you have a good income yourself, you don't feel good living among so many people struggling with poverty," she added.

She expects authorities to restrict internet access again if fighting resumes.

A woman in Tehran described anger toward regime supporters and said another war combined with domestic protests could increase the risk of confrontations on the streets.

Asked about possible attacks on underground nuclear sites, she said the issue felt increasingly detached from her everyday problems.

"What do the nuclear sites have to do with us?" she said. "They are inside mountains."

Edited: Emmy Sasipornkarn

entries.title: Are Europeans putting profits over human rights in Vietnam?
entries.summary: Europe and Vietnam are deepening economic and diplomatic ties, but closer cooperation raises concerns about whether Brussels is doing enough to address Hanoi's human rights record, labor standards and trade imbalances.
entries.content:
Asia

Are Europeans putting profits over human rights in Vietnam?

October 22, 2026

Europe and Vietnam are deepening economic and diplomatic ties, but closer cooperation raises concerns about whether Brussels is doing enough to address Hanoi's human rights record, labor standards and trade imbalances.

Vietnam's Communist Party chief and president, To Lam, arrived in Brussels on Wednesday for an official visit to the European Union (EU) and Belgium in another sign of a relationship that continues to grow. 

The visit comes just days after Vietnam signed a free trade agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), comprising Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

Trade ties between Vietnam and Europe have deepened in recent years. The EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), which took effect in August 2020, substantially expanded Vietnam's commercial ties with most European states.

Amid global tariff wars, the EU-Vietnam relationship "is a welcome advertisement for keeping markets open," Khac Giang Nguyen, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told DW.

"This is a win-win for both sides," he added. "Vietnam offers Europe an established manufacturing base and another foothold in Asian supply chains. Europe offers Vietnam capital, technology and a large market, helping Hanoi reduce its exposure to American demand and Chinese industrial inputs."

Vietnam-EU ties deepen

Vietnam is now the EU's largest goods-trading partner in Southeast Asia and its 14th-largest globally. The EU is Vietnam's fourth-largest trading partner and a major source of foreign investment.

Non-economic relations are also advancing. In January, both sides upgraded ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership — the first such agreement between the EU and a Southeast Asian country.

Vietnam has also become a key strategic partner for the EU in the Indo-Pacific, Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Indo-Pacific international relations at the University of Vienna, told DW.

"The cooperation is crucial for advancing the EU's economic security agenda and its strategy of de-risking from China," he added, referring to Brussels' efforts to diversify its supply chains and reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing.

Several European states have signed defense agreements with Vietnam, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas held talks with Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung on Wednesday to discuss ways to improve security cooperation, including in the South China Sea, where Hanoi is locked in territorial disputes with China.

Concerns over Vietnam's human rights record

However, the relationship has also faced difficulties. Questions remain over whether European companies are benefiting sufficiently from Vietnam's economic boom and whether Brussels is overlooking Hanoi's worsening human rights record.

Vietnam remains a one-party communist state that severely restricts political opposition, independent journalism and civil society. Rights organizations say repression has intensified under To Lam, who previously headed the country's powerful public security ministry.

In an open letter sent this week to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa, 12 international human rights organizations raised "grave concerns over the Vietnamese government's intensifying repression" and urged EU leaders to demand meaningful reforms.

When negotiating the EVFTA and the accompanying political agreements, Hanoi agreed to obligations on human rights, labor protections and environmental standards.

These included commitments to reform labor legislation to permit independent worker organizations and align domestic regulations more closely with International Labour Organization (ILO) standards.

However, rights groups argue that Hanoi has failed to deliver. Vietnam has still not ratified the ILO convention on freedom of association, and independent trade unions remain prohibited.

"The EU has taken no action in response to Vietnam's repeated breaches of its EVFTA-related obligations and pledges; instead, in January it upgraded bilateral relations," the joint letter read.

Benefits 'distributed unevenly'

There are also questions about which Vietnamese companies have benefited most from the EU's trade liberalization.

Large foreign-invested manufacturers and established exporters have been better placed to exploit tariff reductions than smaller domestic businesses, which often lack the resources to navigate Europe's complex import requirements.

Vietnamese exporters also face growing demands from the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and its deforestation regulations, which require businesses in affected sectors to provide more detailed information about their production processes and supply chains.

"It is quite clear that the EVFTA's benefits have been distributed unevenly across sectors, firms, and social groups, while political, regulatory, and economic challenges may complicate the next phase of the relationship," Hai Thiem Bui, a researcher at the Stockholm Center for Global Asia, Stockholm University, told DW.

"The next phase of EU-Vietnam trade relations is likely to depend less on tariff liberalization and more on whether Vietnam can adapt to increasingly demanding EU standards concerning labor rights, sustainability, and regulatory governance," he added.

Better for European firms?

Another challenge concerns how much European businesses are gaining from Vietnam's expanding export economy.

Although the EVFTA has considerably strengthened bilateral commerce, it has been far more successful at increasing Vietnamese exports to Europe than European sales to Vietnam.

The EU's goods-trade deficit with Vietnam reached €51.7 billion ($57.9 billion) in 2025, up from roughly €24 billion in 2019.

This imbalance is becoming more conspicuous as Brussels seeks greater economic security and new export opportunities for European industries.

Another obstacle is the EU-Vietnam Investment Protection Agreement, signed in 2019, which has still not entered into force.

"We have also seen an uptick in investments by European businesses in Vietnam, despite the lack of an Investment Protection Agreement being in place," Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, told DW.

Germany ratified it in February and Poland followed in April, but France, the Netherlands and several other member states have yet to complete ratification.

The agreement will strengthen legal protections for investors and establish a permanent mechanism for resolving investment disputes, potentially encouraging greater European investment in Vietnam.

"With a new government in Vietnam pursuing an ambitious legislative program but with an overall target of maintaining Vietnam's extraordinary growth path, we would expect trade to continue to flourish," Humphrey said.

"That said, many European businesses are looking carefully at what the legislative program may bring in terms of reform," he added.

For Brussels, the next phase of relations is about ensuring that European businesses benefit from that growth, while demonstrating that its commitments to human rights and sustainable trade are more than diplomatic promises.

Edited by: Emmy Sasipornkarn

entries.title: Germany news: Government expecting increased tax revenue in 2027
entries.summary: Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said state tax revenue will increase by €4 billion in 2027. Meanwhile, public service websites have been coming back online after a PHP security scare. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Government expects increased tax revenue in 2027

Published October 22, 2026last updated October 22, 2026

Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said state tax revenue will increase by €4 billion in 2027. Meanwhile, public service websites have been coming back online after a PHP security scare. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • German tax revenues at the federal, state and communal levels are expected to increase in 2027
  • Government and public service websites came down overnight for key PHP patch after security issue was discovered
  • More and more far-right martial arts clubs are opening across Germany
  • Germany has increased its battery storage by 8.2 gigawatt-hours in 2026 so far

Continue reading for a roundup of our Germany coverage on Thursday, October 22, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Government expects billions in extra tax revenue, but budget will remain tight

Government expects billions in extra tax revenue, but budget will remain tight

The German government expects to collect an extra €4.1 billion ($4.6 billion) in taxes next year, according to Finance Ministry calculations released Thursday.

When looking at the federal, state and communal levels, the increase is estimated to be over €10 billion, adding up to a total of €1 trillion paid in taxes in 2027.

However, Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said the increased tax revenue would not bring relief to the budget.

Klingbeil said that despite "international crises and uncertainties," the German government was expecting a "stable trend" in tax revenue for 2026.

"We have responded to these crises. And we are in a robust position," Klingbeil said. For 2027, the government "will not gain any new fiscal leeway overall, but we also won’t have to close any new gaps."

He called for continued consolidation to protect future budgets.

Skip next section German rail's punctuality woes to continue until at least 2029

German rail's punctuality woes to continue until at least 2029

Just wait a little longer. It's a familiar feeling for anyone who's traveled around Germany by train.

According to Deutsche Bahn, it's unlikely that rail travelers in Germany will see any significant improvements to the punctuality issues that plague the network for another few years.

"The knock-on effect will be felt once we have completed the most challenging refurbishment projects," Phillip Nagl, head of Deutsche Bahn subsidiary DB InfraGo, told the weekly newspaper Die Zeit.

One of those major refurbishments is the modernization of the Hamburg-Hanover line, which is scheduled for 2029. Delays and persistent problems have already pushed the schedule back several times.

Richard Lutz, the former head of Deutsche Bahn, claimed in 2024 that the refurbishment of the aging rail network would lead to a steady increase in punctuality. But things have actually gotten worse, with punctuality for long-distance services falling from 64% in 2023 to around 60% in 2025, and this will likely drop again in 2026.

Nagel blamed the delays on outdated infrastructure, with parts of the network breaking down faster than they can be repaired.

Skip next section More than 20 MAN trucks set on fire in Leipzig

More than 20 MAN trucks set on fire in Leipzig

Police are investigating a possible arson attack after more than 20 MAN trucks were set on fire on Thursday evening in the Sellerhausen-Stünz neighborhood of Leipzig, in eastern Germany, local media reported.

The fire broke out around 2 a.m. (0000 GMT) with several vehicles being completely destroyed. The initial estimate of the cost of the damage reached seven figures, according to Radio Leipzig.

The Police Center for Countering Extremism and Terrorism from the Saxony criminal investigation bureau will take over further investigations since a political motive for the arson cannot be ruled out.

The fire services were able to bring the flames under control by morning and there were no report of injuries.

Skip next section Officials warn of continued threats as government sites start coming back online

Officials warn of continued threats as government sites start coming back online

A number of German public service websites were back up and running on Thursday morning after a security vulnerability was discovered in the PHP code that is used to run millions of websites around the world.

However, some state government portals, hospitals and universities were still experiencing online disruptions.

The sites had been taken down as a precaution after the vulnerability was discovered and PHP developers urged users to install a new security patch.

Germany's Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) warned that there was still a threat, especially due to the hackers being able to employ AI to find exploits.

"We consider it likely that there will be widespread exploitation within a few hours of the security updates being released: Attackers can analyze them quickly using AI-powered tools and generate corresponding exploits," the BSI said while recommending a complete disconnection of websites from the internet as long as security cannot be guaranteed.

Experts warned it could take months to fully secure all government, public and private devices, especially those running on outdated software that cannot be fixed with a simple patch.

Skip next section Germany sees rise in far-right martial arts clubs

Germany sees rise in far-right martial arts clubs

There are now 20 known far-right martial art clubs active in Germany, up from around a dozen in June 2024, according to a report from the German government.

The Interior Ministry said there had been a major increase in 2026 in particular. The report came after a parliamentary inquiry by the Greens.

The far right have long used martial arts and fitness to recruit young men into the extremist scene, but the government reported an observed "professionalization of combat skills" among the clubs.

The report said these groups pose threats of violence but no direct confrontations with opposing groups had yet been recorded. It also warned that while it found no evidence of links to similar groups in other countries, this could not be ruled out int he future.

Skip next section Battery storage booming in Germany

Battery storage booming in Germany

Germany has rapidly increased the amount of battery storage it has available, with the number of battery systems increasing by close to half a million between January and September 2026, the solar industry association BSW-Solar reported.

This year's new installations mark an increase of 91% over the same period last year and have a combined storage of 8.2 gigawatt-hours.

That is equivalent to the amount of electricity used by the city of Munich in just under half a day.

A large part of the new battery installations have been large-scale battery systems. The number of systems with a capacity of 1 megawatt or more increased from 63 to 220.

Batteries are a key component of the transition to clean energy that requires the storage of electricity to balance out fluctuations. But BSW-Solar pointed out that a much faster expansion is needed to reach Germany's clean energy goals.

"Battery storage is becoming a driver of growth and efficiency in the energy transition," BSW-Solar managing director Carsten Körnig said, adding that the technology could help save billions in costs.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from a very autumnal Bonn.

Government and public service websites went dark after a major vulnerability was discovered. Some sites have started coming back online after a PHP patch, but officials have warned that it will take time to confirm that hackers did not take advantage of the problem.

We will also be keeping you up to date on the latest from German politics, especially a day after the far-right AfD set out its plans to reduce the power of the EU.

entries.title: India news: Gandhi's nephew forced to pull protest photos
entries.summary: The requested removal of "objectionable" photos from a cultural center took place in state run by Modi's BJP.
entries.content:
India

India news: Gandhi's nephew forced to pull protest photos

Published October 22, 2026last updated October 22, 2026

The requested removal of "objectionable" photos from a cultural center took place in state run by Modi's BJP.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

These updates have been closed.

Below, you can review a roundup of our coverage from India from Thursday, October 22:

  • Rahul Gandhi's nephew was asked to remove 'objectionable' photos depicting the youth protests from an exhibition in New Delhi
  • Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were released from Tihar Jail on Wednesday night
  • The two, calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, were booked for 'trespassing' at Jantar Mantar after it was denotified as a protest site
  • Modi meets Polish PM Donald Tusk, discusses bilateral ties
  • Google, Mozilla, Apple block certificates by Indian company over security flaw
  • Tiger Shroff shooters allegedly surveyed homes of other Bollywood stars

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section These updates have been closed

These updates have been closed

The updates for Thursday, October 22, have been closed. Thank you for joining us.

We'll be back on Friday with more news from India.

Skip next section Gandhi's nephew asked to remove artwork depicting youth protests

Gandhi's nephew asked to remove artwork depicting youth protests

Raihan Vadra, the nephew of Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, was asked to remove a number of photos from an exhibition he was running at a government-run cultural center in New Delhi.

The center, Bikaner House, requested the removal of several pieces of artwork on the grounds that they were "objectionable."

"The photos were of the youth protests in Delhi," Vadra said in a post on social media. "Apparently the content is objectionable."

The Bikaner House Management Society said "certain photographs" from the exhibition were not in line with the center's policies, without elaborating.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP governs Rajasthan state, which is in charge of Bikaner House.

The protest movement has proven to be a major challenge to Modi's power. A recent renewal of the protests, with Rahul Gandhi at its forefront, has seen protesters calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner ‌Gyanesh ​Kumar over a controversial revision of voter lists.

Skip next section Amit Shah criticizes opposition over 'vote theft' protests

Amit Shah criticizes opposition over 'vote theft' protests

Union Home Minister Amit Shah criticized Congress and the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) on Thursday over allegations of electoral irregularities, saying protests and demonstrations would not help them win elections, the Hindustan Times reported.

Speaking at an event in Delhi, Shah accused the opposition of using allegations of "vote theft" to challenge the Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) electoral victories.

Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has claimed that India's election authority had enabled "vote theft," or manipulation of electoral rolls to favor Modi's BJP in the 2024 general elections.

Currently, the opposition along with the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and other student organizations are demanding the resignation of the country's controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were removed from draft electoral rolls nationwide.

Meanwhile, separately, BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia accused Gandhi of links with foreign-based organizations that he alleged were amplifying protests in India, the Times of India newspaper reported.

Bhatia alleged that the organizations were part of a wider effort to create unrest and undermine constitutional institutions, and demanded that Gandhi disclose details of his meetings with them, the report said.

Skip next section One Indian killed, three injured in attacks on Saudi airport, oilfield

One Indian killed, three injured in attacks on Saudi airport, oilfield

One Indian national was killed and two others injured in an attack on Dammam airport in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, while another Indian national was injured in an attack on the Shaybah oil field, the Indian foreign ministry said in a statement on Thursday.

The Wednesday evening attack in the Saudi Arabian city of Dammam killed two people and eight others in total, the country's aviation authority said on Thursday.

In a separate attack on Wednesday, two people were killed by debris from an intercepted drone launched by the Iran-backed Houthis targeting the Shaybah oil field operated by state energy giant Aramco, Saudi media reported.

The US embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert on Wednesday about possible further attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia.

"We strongly condemn the continued attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, including the attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field in the Eastern Province on October 21," the Indian foreign ministry statement said.

"These attacks have unfortunately resulted in civilian deaths and injuries," India's foreign ministry said.

Skip next section Modi meets Polish PM Donald Tusk, discusses bilateral ties

Modi meets Polish PM Donald Tusk, discusses bilateral ties

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Polish counterpart Donald Tusk held talks in New Delhi on Thursday to review bilateral ties and explore cooperation in trade, defense and technology, media reports said.

"Our growing economic strength has created new opportunities for the India-Poland partnership. And the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement has made these opportunities even broader," Modi said while addressing the joint press meet with Tusk.

Tusk said the friendship between New Delhi and Warsaw is not based merely on diplomatic relations, but on the "shared heritage of humanity and empathy."

The two leaders oversaw the exchange of several memorandums of understanding.

Tusk is on a two-day trip to India ending on Friday. He is accompanied by Polish Minister of Finance and Economy, Andrzej Domanski, and a business delegation.

On Wednesday, Tusk met Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar where the two discussed ways to deepen bilateral cooperation, according to reports.

Skip next section Tiger Shroff shooters allegedly surveyed homes of other Bollywood stars

Tiger Shroff shooters allegedly surveyed homes of other Bollywood stars

Authorities investigating last week's shooting at actor Tiger Shroff's car said the alleged shooters had conducted reconnaissance at the homes of Bollywood stars Salman Khan, Aamir Khan and Ranbir Kapoor before targeting Shroff, who they believed had less security, the Indian Express newspaper reported.

This comes even as three more people were arrested in connection with the shooting, Mumbai Police said.

The total number of people arrested related to the case has now risen to 10.

Three motorcycle-borne assailants had opened fire at Shroff's car in the western city of Mumbai on October 18. The actor escaped unhurt, while his driver and a bystander were injured.

Three key accused, including the alleged shooters, were caught by the police while trying to escape to Nepal.

Police suspect the attack was carried out at the behest of Anil Pandit, an alleged operative of the Lawrence Bishnoi gang.

The Bishnoi gang, accused of involvement in the 2023 killing of Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada, has claimed responsibility for the attack.

Bishnoi, a jailed Indian gangster, has been accused by US prosecutors of directing murders, extortion and international drug trafficking from inside a prison in Gujarat.

Skip next section Google, Mozilla, Apple block certificates by Indian company over security flaw

Google, Mozilla, Apple block certificates by Indian company over security flaw

Bengaluru-based digital identity and cybersecurity company eMudhra has revoked eight intermediate certificates after their private keys were found to be weak, prompting Google, Mozilla, Apple and Microsoft to block the affected certificates.

"Eight intermediate (issuing) CAs in our Global TLS business were revoked because their published keys were weak," the company said, adding that it was investigating the issue.

A certificate authority (CA) is an organization that browsers such as Chrome, Firefox and Safari rely on to verify website identities and establish secure connections.

The flaw could have allowed attackers to impersonate legitimate websites using fraudulent certificates and potentially intercept or manipulate supposedly secure online communications. However, no evidence of such misuse has been publicly confirmed.

The flaw originated in a key-generation process in April 2025 that produced weak private keys, the company said.

Media reports citing security researcher Scott Helme said one of the keys was the number four, rather than a cryptographically secure, randomly generated number, while others were also easily guessable.

India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) said it had taken serious note of the incident.

"A special team has been constituted to investigate the matter," the ministry said in a statement on X.

Skip next section CJP leaders freed after undertaking not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar

CJP leaders freed after undertaking not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were released from Tihar Jail on Wednesday after a Special Executive Magistrate declined a police request to extend their judicial custody by three more days, reports said.

The two leaders at the forefront of the protests calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar following voter-list irregularities, furnished personal bonds and sureties of Rs 50,000 (€470; $530) each.

Their written undertakings promised to maintain peace and not call for protests at Jantar Mantar "till such a time that it is denotified in accordance with law."

The iconic protest site was denotified by Delhi Police earlier in October, months after CJP-led protests culminated in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Das and Ranka were booked for "trespassing" after entering the Jantar Mantar protest site and raising the Indian flag.

The latest CJP protests have called for Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the deletion of voters' names.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage!

Welcome to our coverage!

Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi bureau bringing you the latest updates from across India.

First things first: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka are out of judicial custody — after agreeing not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar.

Meanwhile, talking about cybersecurity scares, Indian certificate authority eMudhra confirmed a flaw that prompted Google, Mozilla, Apple and Microsoft to block its vulnerable certificates and some Indian government websites to go offline.

For all this and more, follow our live blog.

entries.title: France confirms first Shamonda virus infection in a human death of 'severely immunocompromised' individual
entries.summary: The Shamonda virus has been detected in a human for the first time, French health officials said. Authorities see no risk to the public, adding that the victim, who died in early October, was severely immunocompromised.
entries.content:
October 22, 2026

The Shamonda virus has been detected in a human for the first time, French health officials said. Authorities see no risk to the public, adding that the victim, who died in early October, was severely immunocompromised.

French health officials on Thursday confirmed that they had detected the Shamonda virus in a human — who died early this month — in what they say was the first-ever case of a human contracting the livestock disease.

"Despite circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, the Shamonda virus has never previously been detected in humans," said France's Ministries of Health and of Agriculture in a joint statement.

"No health risk to the general public identified at this time," they said, adding that the human infection appeared to be, "an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient."

The World Health Organization (WHO) said the virus was unlikely to spread. 

"Based on current information and knowledge of ‌the transmission of closely related ‌viruses, ​this is an isolated human case and it is unlikely to ​lead to wider spread at this time," WHO told ⁠Reuters ​in a ​statement.

How is Shamonda virus transmitted?

First ​identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, the insect-borne Shamonda virus is a variant of the Orthobunyavirus, a genus that contains 138 species, and primarily affects livestock, ‌particularly cattle.

It is transmitted by culicoides, or biting midges.

The virus has been detected in ​animals in Africa and Japan for years and has been spreading across Europe this year.

Until now, it was not thought to be transmissible to humans.

According to a press statement on the Ministry of Agriculture's webpage, "At this stage of the investigation, the hypothesis is that the case resulted from vector-borne transmission via the bite of a culicoid midge in eastern France, a region where the virus was reported to be circulating among animals in the spring and summer of 2026."

The ministry said biological, clinical and epidemiological investigations are being carried out by experts in human, animal and environmental health, adding that authorities at the WHO and European Center for Disease Control had been notified of the incident.

entries.title: Iran's Balochistan border region sees growing unrest
entries.summary: Violence is on the rise in Iran's border region with Afghanistan and Pakistan. The Iran war could shift the strategic balance for militant groups operating in the area.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Iran's Balochistan border region sees growing unrest

October 22, 2026

Violence is on the rise in Iran's border region with Afghanistan and Pakistan. The Iran war could shift the strategic balance for militant groups operating in the area.

Recent weeks have seen renewed attacks, assassinations and armed clashes in the southeastern province bordering Pakistan and Afghanistan. The incidents occurred in the provincial capital of Zahedan, as well as smaller border towns.

The border region of Iran, Pakistan and Afghanistan is home to the Baloch ethnic minority. The region on either side of the Iran-Pakistan border is among the most economically disadvantaged of the wider area.

The Pakistani province of Balochistan is economically underdeveloped, despite having large reserves of natural gas, gold and copper.

The situation is similarly dire in the Iranian province of Sistan and Baluchistan, which is predominantly inhabited by Sunni Baluchis. It is one of the poorest regions in the country and marked by underdeveloped infrastructure, limited educational opportunities and water supply shortages.

Significantly less information is available about the situation of the Baloch in Afghanistan.

Armed groups sense security gaps

Various Baloch groups are active in Iran and Pakistan, some of whom seek Balochistan independence. Yet to date, there is no evidence of coordinated cross-border cooperation among these organizations.

In December 2025, several Baloch opposition groups in Iran united under the umbrella of the Popular Fighters Front. Observers see this as an attempt to more closely integrate their political and military activities.

This coalition, which formed before the outbreak of the Iran war, could try to exploit security gaps created by the current situation, Iranian journalist Mehdi Nakhl Ahmadi told DW.

Ahmadi, who lives in Italy, has been covering the situation of the Baloch people for years. He said the new security situation could allow armed groups to expand their operations.

Struggling with poverty, suffering marginalization

Ahmadi said there are structural reasons for Baloch dissatisfaction. "The Islamic Republic's security policy toward ethnic and religious regions has widened the gap in economic development between these regions and other parts of the country in recent decades," he said.

He added that the rising number of attacks points to a shift in dynamics, as do increased coordination and changes in the way recent operations have been carried out.

Among the victims of recent clashes were members of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the Basij militia, armed individuals, and a Sunni cleric.

A source within Iran, who is familiar with the situation of the Baloch people, yet whose identity we cannot disclose security for reasons, attributed some of the armed violence to political, economic and religious discontent.

Discrimination in employment, education, regional development and religious matters contribute to the tension, the source said.

That's why the armed conflict should not be viewed in isolation, the Iranian source explained. Clergy, academics and other social leaders had been trying for years to peacefully voice their demands for better social policies and greater investment in the region, the source said.

The fact that these efforts were largely unsuccessful had led to a growing willingness among some to resort to more radical measures.

"The high number of executions in recent decades is another factor that fuels discontent," said the source. Most documented executions in the province, meanwhile, are related to drug offenses.

Although Baluchis make only up an estimated 2–6% of the Iranian population, they are significantly overrepresented among those put to death. Iran Human Rights reports that Baluchis accounted for 9% of all recorded executions in 2025. In previous years, that figure was 11% (2024) and 20% (2023), respectively.

For many people who live in this economically disadvantaged region, smuggling opium into Iran, and fuel out of the country, are one of the few ways to earn a living. This, in turn, has contributed to a continued military and security presence at the border.

It is not, meanwhile, known whether armed groups in southeastern Iran are being supported from abroad.

Violence has also escalated in the Pakistani province of Balochistan. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, 131 armed attacks were recorded there in September, up from 89 in August.

In addition to the separatist movement, which has been active for years, the Pakistani Taliban (TTP) are also expanding their operations. This had led to strategically important transportation links between Iran and Pakistan coming under growing pressure.

Still, it cannot be said with certainty whether the recent uptick in violence in Iran's Sistan and Baluchistan province stems from security gaps resulting from the Iran war.

The growing number of attacks does, however, suggests that the security situation in the already fragile border region continues to deteriorate.

Additional reporting by Morad Rahmati.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Ukraine: Life near the front line in Sloviansk
entries.summary: As Russian continues to attack Sloviansk in eastern Ukraine, thousands of residents refuse to leave or struggle to find a way out. For many, poverty, family ties and beloved pets make evacuation painfully difficult.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Russia's war in Ukraine: Life near the front line in Sloviansk

October 22, 2026

As Russian continues to attack Sloviansk in eastern Ukraine, thousands of residents refuse to leave or struggle to find a way out. For many, poverty, family ties and beloved pets make evacuation painfully difficult.

A few days ago, three Russian aerial bombs struck a residential neighborhood on the outskirts of Sloviansk. One hit a five-story apartment building, injuring seven people. Along with neighboring Kramatorsk, Sloviansk is one of the last major towns in the eastern Ukrainian region of Donetsk still under Ukrainian control. Since summer, the city has been a combat zone.

In a courtyard surrounded by damaged apartment blocks, a dusty carpet hangs over the metal frame of a swing set. Tetjana, a pensioner who lives in the building across the street, has brought it out of her rubble-strewn apartment to clean it. She was in her kitchen when the bombs struck.

"The bomb hit the second floor, and a woman who lived on the fourth floor was screaming," she tells DW. "They managed to rescue her before that entire section of the building collapsed," she adds.

Despite being offered the opportunity to evacuate, Tetjana has yet to leave Sloviansk. "I don't know where I would go," she says. Rent can cost up to €400 ($449) a month. Tetjana's pension is the equivalent of just €67 ($75) a month. Even with monthly relocation assistance of about €40 ($45), she could not make ends meet. "I couldn't live on that. Nowhere!"

Meanwhile, electricity and water are still available in her neighborhood, but the gas supply has been cut off. "We'll get through this," Tetjana says hopefully. "Everything will be OK. That's what I tell everyone. I want that so much."

Residents reluctant to evacuate without pets

Days after the attack, the few residents remaining in the damaged buildings were still clearing out their apartments. But another attack hit as they worked. This time, the bombs struck a building housing a state-run emergency assistance center and the Red Cross. While firefighters put out the blaze, rescue workers and volunteers retrieved belongings left inside and cleared away broken glass. Eight people were injured in the attack.

"I was on the balcony when there was a deafening bang. It felt as if someone had hit me over the head," says Natalja, describing one of the recent attacks. The pensioner comes to this part of the city to care for her twin sister. "She can no longer get around. Today, I couldn't bring her bread, only crispbread," she tells DW. Although shops and a few stalls remain at the burned-out market, bread is not available every day.

"I tried to persuade my sister to leave. I would go to a nursing home and she would go to a hospital. But her dog is sick, and I have one, too," Natalja says, noting that pets are not allowed during evacuations. "I can't leave my sister behind. She is worried and angry with me, as if everything were my fault. I have no strength left."

Natalja slowly sets off for home, "so I can get there before dark." The city center is nearly 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) away. Public transportation has been suspended since 30 people were killed in an attack on two buses in neighboring Kramatorsk.

"We're used to living under fire"

The center of Sloviansk is heavily damaged. Few people are out on the streets, though a handful of shops remain open. Of the city's 100,000 residents, about 20,000 remain, most of them elderly people who are unable to leave.

Vasyl, a pensioner, is from the village of Mayaky, north of Sloviansk. A neighbor drove him into the city center, where he sat down for lunch in a cafe. "We're used to living under fire by now," he says. "But it's a bad habit. We should have broken it long ago."

Vasyl wants peace for his homeland. But he rejects Russian President Vladimir Putin's demand that the part of the Donetsk region under Ukrainian control be handed over to Moscow.

Two elderly women talk on a street covered with nets to protect against drones. "I can't remember the last time I slept through the night," says Iryna, a pensioner. "It's terrible, but I have nowhere to go. I'm supposed to leave my two cats behind, but I love them so much. They're all I have."

"We can only hide, trembling, and pray to God that everything will be all right," Iryna continues. "When I have to go to the market, I don't know if I'll make it there alive."

Russian drones attacked the central market several weeks ago, injuring at least three people. Since then, fewer vendors and customers have been coming to the market.

"We dream of staying here"

Valeriya sells women's underwear. With kindergartens closed, she has to bring her 5-year-old daughter Sofia to work. Their neighborhood in Sloviansk is not yet subject to the mandatory evacuation of families with children.

"We're used to this life by now. We were evacuated in 2022, but later returned. Now we're waiting to be evacuated again," Valeriya says.

Sofia races through the market aisles with her friend Anya, who is a year older. Anya's mother is a soldier defending her hometown. Her grandmother, Tetjana, sits nearby selling men's clothing. She, too, has to look after her granddaughter while working.

Tetjana has started shipping her belongings to the Dnipropetrovsk region, where she hopes to start a new life. She is sending them while the post office is still open. "It hurts to see our Ukraine being destroyed," she says, fighting back tears. "Who will rebuild our cities?"

She hopes to return one day. But the fate of Bakhmut weighs on her mind. "Look at Bakhmut. There are no houses left. I'm counting on our boys to hold our cities, even though it's very difficult." Bakhmut, about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from Sloviansk, fell to Russian forces in 2023 after months of heavy fighting.

The women see little hope for a ceasefire. "Putin won't want one. And our younger generation will ask us what we fought for in the first place," Tetjana says. She believes Russia must withdraw from Ukrainian territory.

Drones buzz overhead as gunfire echoes across the market. "It's hard for our boys to shoot them down," Tetjana says. "But they're doing their best."

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

entries.title: Germany arrests Ukrainian man suspected of spying for Russia
entries.summary: The suspect is thought to have gathered defense-related information on the production of tanks and munitions, as well as details about NATO's eastern flank.
entries.content:
October 22, 2026

The suspect is thought to have gathered defense-related information on the production of tanks and munitions, as well as details about NATO's eastern flank.

Police in the  German state of Brandenburg have arrested a Ukrainian man on suspicion of spying for Russia, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office in Karlsruhe said Thursday.

The man, identified only as Vadym Y. by prosecutors, is suspected of having used his connections to European defense firms to gather information that he then allegedly passed on to a Russian spy agency.

What do we know about the alleged espionage in Germany?

Prosecutors said he had been in touch with a middleman since July 2025. They said he had been gathering intelligence in connection with the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine from Germany.

This information reportedly included "details regarding the production of armored vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as information on personnel and military facilities at locations intended to secure NATO's eastern flank."

Germany has been on high alert for acts of sabotage in recent months, especially since an explosive-laden drone was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport. Berlin said Moscow was behind the attempted attack.

Why is Germany worried about Russia's 'hybrid' war?

Germany is one of the biggest military and political supporters of Ukraine, especially following an increasingly friendly US stance toward Russia under President Donald Trump.

This seems to have put Germany in Russia's crosshairs as part of what has been called a "hybrid" campaign of espionage, sabotage and other disruptions.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was not surprised by the arrest, adding that there would be more such cases ⁠in ​the future.

Besides the incident at Leipzig airport, there have been numerous cases of people being arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. Moscow has denied all allegations.

This has led Germany to give increased powers to its own spying agency, the BND.

The agency's chief, Martin Jaeger, told German lawmakers earlier in October that the Russian "shadow war" is escalating and has "taken on a new, more dangerous character."

"Germany is at risk of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia," he told a hearing of parliament's intelligence oversight committee in Berlin.

Edited by: Zac Crellin
